chunks: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about something from the (divine) attributes. So he raised his hand toward the sky, then said: Exalted is the Compeller! Exalted is the Compeller! Whoever ventures into what is there (beyond) is destroyed.

key_terms.الجبار: Al-Jabbar — one of the Beautiful Names of God, meaning the Compeller, the All-Mighty, the Irresistible
key_terms.الصفة: Divine attribute — referring to the qualities of God such as knowledge, power, and will
key_terms.تعاطى: Ventures into/attempts — refers to theological speculation about the inner nature of divine attributes
key_terms.تعالى: Exalted/transcendent — a declaration of God's absolute transcendence above created things
key_terms.هلك: Is destroyed/perishes — spiritual ruin resulting from transgressing proper epistemic limits

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about discussing divine attributes in Islam?
ai.summary: Abd al-Rahman ibn Atik al-Qasir narrates that when he asked Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) about the divine attributes, the Imam responded not with theological elaboration but with a dramatic gesture — raising his hand to the sky — and an emphatic exclamation declaring the transcendence of God (al-Jabbar, the Compeller). The repetition of 'Exalted is the Compeller' underscores that God's essence is utterly beyond human comprehension. The warning that 'whoever ventures into what is there is destroyed' reflects the classical Shia theological position that speculating about the inner nature (kayfiyya) of the divine attributes leads one to spiritual ruin, and is the context of this chapter: the forbiddance of speaking about 'how' (al-kayf) with respect to God.
